questions.stem: The work done on an object by a constant force is the scalar product of:
questions.explanation: Work is defined as the dot product of force and displacement.

questions.explanation: Only the component F cos θ along displacement contributes to work.

questions.stem: The component of force that directly contributes to work along displacement is:
questions.explanation: The effective component parallel to displacement is F cos θ.

questions.explanation: The SI unit of work is the joule (J).

questions.explanation: 1 J = 1 N m.

questions.explanation: For parallel force and displacement, θ = 0° and cos θ = 1.

questions.stem: When θ = 90°, the work done by the force is:
questions.explanation: cos 90° = 0, so W = 0.

questions.stem: When θ = 180°, the work done is:
questions.explanation: cos 180° = -1, so W = -Fd.

questions.explanation: The cosine is positive for acute angles from 0° to less than 90°.

questions.stem: Negative work occurs for:

questions.stem: Zero work due to angular orientation occurs when force is:
questions.explanation: A perpendicular force has no component along the displacement.

questions.explanation: With zero displacement, W = Fd cos θ = 0.

questions.stem: If the force is doubled while d and θ remain unchanged, the work becomes:
questions.explanation: W is directly proportional to F.

questions.stem: If the displacement is doubled while F and θ remain unchanged, the work becomes:
questions.explanation: W is directly proportional to d.

questions.stem: The region around a body where it can influence other bodies by an associated force is called a:
questions.explanation: A force field is the region in which an associated force can act.

questions.stem: Which of the following is named in the textbook as a force field?
questions.explanation: Gravitational field is one of the textbook examples.

questions.stem: Which set contains only force fields named in Topic 5.2?
questions.explanation: The textbook names electric, viscous and gravitational fields.

questions.stem: A field is conservative if work between two fixed points is:
questions.explanation: Path independence is the first conservative-field property.

questions.stem: For a conservative field, work done around any closed path is:
questions.explanation: Closed-path work is zero for a conservative field.

questions.stem: Which is a conservative field according to the textbook?
questions.explanation: Gravitational field is explicitly identified as conservative.

questions.stem: Which is also a conservative field according to the textbook?
questions.explanation: Electric field is explicitly identified as conservative.

questions.stem: Which force is conservative?
questions.explanation: Gravitational force is conservative.

questions.stem: Which force is non-conservative?
questions.explanation: Frictional force is a textbook example of a non-conservative force.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-conservative force?
questions.explanation: Viscous drag is non-conservative.

questions.stem: Air resistance is classified as:
questions.explanation: Air resistance is listed as a non-conservative force.

questions.stem: In a conservative field, two different paths from A to B give:
questions.explanation: Work is independent of the path taken.

questions.stem: In a non-conservative field, work between the same two points generally:

options.text: is always equal for all paths

questions.explanation: Path dependence characterizes non-conservative behaviour.

questions.stem: A path for which the beginning and ending points are the same is called a:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of a closed path used in the topic.

questions.stem: If W(A→B, Path I) = W(A→B, Path II) for alternative routes, the observation is consistent with:
questions.explanation: Equal work for different routes is consistent with path independence.

questions.stem: If W(A→B, Path I) ≠ W(A→B, Path II), the force is:
questions.explanation: Different work for the same endpoints means path dependence.

questions.stem: Which equation represents a conservative closed path?
questions.explanation: For a conservative field the total work around any closed path is zero.

questions.stem: Which equation best represents path independence?
questions.explanation: Equal work for different paths between the same endpoints expresses path independence.

questions.stem: The decisive feature for classifying a field in Topic 5.2 is the behaviour of:
questions.explanation: Conservative/non-conservative classification is based on how work behaves.

questions.stem: Frictional field is non-conservative because work done against friction:
questions.explanation: The textbook explicitly gives path dependence as the reason.

questions.explanation: Gravitational and electric forces are conservative.

questions.stem: Which pair contains two non-conservative examples?
questions.explanation: Friction and air resistance are both non-conservative.

questions.explanation: All three are listed as non-conservative.

questions.stem: If an object returns to its starting point under a conservative force, the net work by that force is:
questions.explanation: The trip is a closed path, so total work is zero.

questions.explanation: Non-zero closed-path work violates the conservative condition.

questions.stem: Which statement is true for conservative forces?
questions.explanation: Path independence is the key property.

questions.stem: Which statement is true for non-conservative forces?
questions.explanation: Non-conservative work depends on path.
